title: High Tibial Osteotomy (HTO): Can an Osteotomy Save My Knee Instead of a Knee Replacement?
seoTitle: High Tibial Osteotomy (HTO) vs Knee Replacement
metaDescription: Who suits a high tibial osteotomy, what it involves, recovery time, how long it lasts, and how it compares with partial or total knee replacement.
intro: If you are in your 40s or 50s, active, and told your knee arthritis is mostly on the inner side, you may have heard the word "osteotomy". It is not a replacement: it keeps your own joint and changes how weight passes through it. It suits a fairly narrow group of people well, and many others not at all. This guide explains who fits, what recovery really involves, and what the research says about how long it lasts.
summary: A high tibial osteotomy (HTO) cuts and realigns the shin bone just below the knee so that body weight shifts away from a worn inner (medial) compartment. It is mainly for younger, active, bow-legged adults with arthritis on one side only. It can delay a knee replacement for years, but many people still need one later.

sections.heading: What does a high tibial osteotomy actually do?
sections.body:
An HTO straightens a bow-legged knee by reshaping the top of the shin bone (tibia). That moves load from the worn inner side of the knee to the healthier outer side, easing pressure where the cartilage has thinned. Your own joint, ligaments and cartilage stay in place; nothing is replaced with metal or plastic.

According to AAOS OrthoInfo, the bone is either opened as a wedge on the inner side (medial opening wedge) or a wedge is removed from the outer side (lateral closing wedge). In both, the bone is then held with a plate or similar fixation while it heals. The aim is to relieve pain and protect the remaining good cartilage, not to rebuild what has already worn away.
bullets: Opening wedge: a cut on the inner side is gently opened and fixed with a plate
Closing wedge: a small wedge of bone is removed from the outer side and the gap closed
Either way, the leg ends up slightly straighter or very mildly knock-kneed

sections.heading: Am I a candidate for an osteotomy?
sections.body:
The typical candidate is under about 60, active, not overweight, and has pain only on the inner side of the knee from bow-legged alignment. AAOS OrthoInfo describes knee osteotomy as most effective for thin, active patients under 60 whose pain is on one side of the knee and comes mainly with activity or long periods of standing.

OrthoInfo also notes that candidates should be able to straighten the knee fully and bend it to at least 90 degrees, and that people with rheumatoid arthritis are not good candidates. Arthritis spread across the whole knee, or pain behind the kneecap, usually points elsewhere. Age is a guide rather than a rule: your X-rays, alignment, ligaments and goals all matter. A standing full-leg X-ray is normally needed to measure alignment properly.
bullets: Good fit: pain on the inner side only, bow legs, active lifestyle, good knee movement
Poor fit: arthritis in all compartments, inflammatory arthritis, a stiff knee, kneecap arthritis
Not needed at all: mild arthritis that is controlled with exercise, weight loss and activity changes

sections.heading: What is recovery like after HTO?
sections.body:
Recovery is slower than many people expect, because the cut bone has to heal. AAOS OrthoInfo states that most patients go home one to two days after surgery, use crutches for several weeks, and that the bone takes about six weeks to heal. Full activities may be possible around three to six months after surgery.

Your surgeon decides when you can put full weight on the leg, depending on the type of osteotomy and how the bone is healing on X-ray. Physiotherapy to regain movement and strength is a big part of the result. Plan time off work, especially if your job involves standing, climbing or driving long distances.

Seek prompt care if you develop increasing calf pain or swelling, chest pain or breathlessness, fever, redness or discharge from the wound, or numbness or coldness in the foot. OrthoInfo lists infection, blood clots, stiffness, nerve or vessel injury and failure of the bone to heal among the possible complications.

sections.heading: How long does an osteotomy last before I need a replacement?
sections.body:
An HTO often buys several years, sometimes much longer, but it is a delaying operation for many people rather than a permanent cure. Studies measure "survival" as the time before the knee is converted to a knee replacement, and the figures vary between studies and patient groups.

A 2017 meta-analysis in Scientific Reports found pooled survival of about 95% for opening wedge and 94% for closing wedge HTO at 5 years, and about 92% and 85% respectively at 10 years. For closing wedge HTO, survival at 15 years was about 75%. A 2024 systematic review in Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery, looking at patients with more advanced medial arthritis on X-ray, reported an average 10-year survival of 74.6%, with a wide range across studies (60% to 98.1%).

These are averages from selected patients, not a prediction for any one knee. AAOS OrthoInfo notes that a previous osteotomy can make a later total knee replacement more challenging in some cases, which is worth discussing before you decide.

sections.heading: How does HTO compare with partial or total knee replacement?
sections.body:
The choice depends mostly on your age, activity level, where the arthritis is, and your leg alignment. HTO keeps your own knee and suits younger, active people with one-sided wear and bow legs. Partial and total replacements remove worn surfaces and are more often used when arthritis is more advanced or in older patients.

sections.heading: When is an osteotomy not the right answer?
sections.body:
An osteotomy is not the right choice if your arthritis is mild and manageable, spread across the whole knee, or caused by inflammatory disease, or if your main goal is the most predictable pain relief at an older age. Many people with early medial arthritis do well for years with strengthening, weight management and activity changes.

If non-surgical care is still working, there is no rush. If it is not, an assessment with standing X-rays will show whether your knee falls into the group where osteotomy makes sense, or whether a replacement, or simply continued conservative care, is more suitable.

faqs.q: Is high tibial osteotomy an alternative to knee replacement?
faqs.a: For selected younger, active people with bow legs and arthritis on the inner side only, yes. It keeps your own joint and can delay a replacement for years, though many people eventually need one.

faqs.q: How long is recovery after HTO?
faqs.a: AAOS OrthoInfo describes crutches for several weeks, about six weeks for the bone to heal, and a return to full activities around three to six months after surgery.

faqs.q: How long does a high tibial osteotomy last?
faqs.a: It varies. A 2017 meta-analysis found roughly 92% of opening wedge and 85% of closing wedge osteotomies had not been converted to a replacement at 10 years. Results in more advanced arthritis can be lower.

faqs.q: Can I have a knee replacement after an osteotomy?
faqs.a: Yes. A replacement can be done later if needed, although AAOS OrthoInfo notes that a previous osteotomy can make the operation more challenging in some cases.

faqs.q: Am I too old for an osteotomy?
faqs.a: AAOS OrthoInfo describes it as most effective in thin, active people under 60. Age is a guide, not a fixed cut-off; alignment, where the arthritis is, knee movement and your goals matter as much.
